375.bp: The ordinary object here is a person opening YouTube and being handed a next video by the platform rather than by a deliberate search. Because the abstract says more than 70 percent of YouTube viewing comes through recommendations, those next-video choices are not a side feature; they are a large part of how political information is encountered. The paper asks whether that choice process behaves differently for YouTube Shorts than for long videos. This matters because a short clip and a longer segment can carry the same news story while inviting different viewing habits, pacing, and follow-up recommendations. The study serves platform auditing: it tries to observe what a closed recommendation system actually exposes people to, especially political content, without seeing the platform's internal rules. The central public question is not simply whether Shorts are popular, but whether the Shorts recommendation path gives users a different political information diet than the long-form path.
375.wh: The hard part is that a recommender is both hidden and reactive. Researchers can see the videos it returns, but not the internal reasons those videos were chosen. A simple comparison between all Shorts and all long videos would be unfair, because the two pools may differ in topic, creator, audience, length, and publishing style before the recommendation system acts. Political exposure is also not one measurement. The audit has to ask whether recommended videos are political at all, whether the set of returned videos is diverse or repetitive, how much engagement those videos receive, and whether their political alignment follows the seed video. Each measure can move differently. A system might recommend fewer political videos but a narrower set, or many political videos from mixed sides. The scale matters too: individual recommendation chains are noisy, so the paper collects 50,000 paired recommendations to separate a pattern from chance.
375.naive: A smart beginner might pick a few political videos, open YouTube, record the recommended Shorts and long videos nearby, and judge by inspection whether one side looks more polarizing. That fails for two reasons. First, the starting videos may not be comparable: one long video could be a detailed interview while a Short from another source could be a provocative clip, so the observed difference may come from the seed rather than the algorithm. Second, small manual samples confuse accident with structure. A few recommendations can be shaped by timing, popularity, or random availability. The beginner might also count only political recommendations, but that would miss diversity, engagement, and alignment, which are separate ways a recommendation path can narrow or amplify a political diet.
375.ap: The paper's central move is to make the comparison fair before measuring the outcomes. It uses the fact that many news organizations publish both short and long versions of the same content. That creates matched starting points: two seeds tied to the same source and likely the same story, but placed into different YouTube recommendation systems. From those matched seeds, the audit collects pairs of recommendations from political and nonpolitical starting videos. It then compares the recommendation outputs along several concrete dimensions: how often political videos appear, how varied the retrieved videos are, how much engagement those recommended videos receive, and how closely the recommended videos line up politically with the seed. The method is not trying to guess YouTube's internal code. It treats YouTube as a system that can be probed through carefully controlled inputs and observed outputs, then asks whether the short-form and long-form paths lead to meaningfully different exposure patterns.
375.mech: The mechanism begins with seed videos, which are the starting items fed to YouTube's recommendation system. The important design choice is matching: when a news organization has a short and a long version of related content, those two seeds act like a controlled pair. One side enters the Shorts recommendation path and the other enters the long-form recommendation path. The audit includes both political and nonpolitical seeds so it can see whether political exposure appears only after political starts or also leaks into broader viewing. For each seed, the researchers collect recommended videos, producing 50,000 pairs of long-form and short-form recommendations. Each recommendation is then described by properties relevant to polarization. One property is whether it is political. Another is diversity: whether the system retrieves a broad set of videos or keeps returning a narrow collection. A third is engagement, meaning the visible audience response those recommended videos receive. A fourth is partisan alignment, meaning whether the recommended video's political leaning matches the seed video's leaning. After those properties are assigned, the audit compares the two sides of each matched pair. The output is not a personalized user model; it is a measurement map showing how recommendation behavior differs between Shorts and long-form videos under comparable starting conditions.
375.math: The main mathematical idea is matched comparison. In plain terms, if two cases are alike in the important starting facts but differ in one chosen condition, then differences in their outcomes are more informative. Here the matched cases are short and long versions from news organizations, and the chosen condition is the recommendation format. This does not reveal every internal cause, but it reduces a major source of confusion: content differences between unrelated videos. The audit also uses counting and proportions. Counting political recommendations estimates exposure frequency: out of many returned videos, what share are political? Diversity measurement asks how spread out the returned set is rather than treating every count as equally healthy; a list of many repeats is different from a list drawn from many sources. Engagement measurement treats views, likes, comments, or similar signals as traces of audience response, while recognizing that engagement is not the same as agreement. Alignment measurement compares the political direction of a seed with that of a recommendation. Underneath all of these is sampling under uncertainty. One recommendation is weak evidence; 50,000 paired recommendations make repeated patterns harder to dismiss as accidental. The tradeoff is control versus realism: the audit controls seed matching, but it still observes a live platform from the outside.
375.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of recommendation, social influence, and trust auditing. It is a recommender-systems paper because the object being studied is the choice of a small set of next videos from a huge catalog. It connects to social-network and influence work because the consequence is political exposure: recommendation lists can help shape what communities repeatedly see, which voices become familiar, and whether users are nudged toward politically aligned material. It also belongs near misinformation and platform-accountability papers because the method is an audit, not a new ranking algorithm. In the repo's current data, nearby YouTube audit work asks whether user controls such as dislike or not-interested buttons actually change downstream recommendations, and another YouTube audit project focuses on reproducible ways to simulate users. This paper takes a different branch of the same deeper problem: hold the platform partly constant, vary the video format, and measure whether the recommendation pathway itself changes the information diet.
375.ww: The approach should work better than the naive comparison because it attacks the biggest source of unfairness in the measurement. If unrelated Shorts and long videos are compared, format is tangled with topic, creator, audience, and production style. Matching short and long versions from the same news organization narrows that gap, so differences in recommendations are more likely to reflect the two recommendation systems rather than entirely different starting material. The large collection of paired recommendations also turns the audit from anecdote into repeated observation. A single surprising recommendation says little; many matched pairs can reveal stable differences in political frequency, diversity, engagement, or alignment. The multiple measurements matter because polarization is not a single visible event. A system can polarize by showing more political content, by reducing variety, by favoring already high-engagement material, or by keeping users close to the seed's political side. Looking across these dimensions gives a richer picture of exposure dynamics than simply asking whether the next video looks extreme.
375.po: The payoff is a concrete audit of a growing part of YouTube that the abstract says had been understudied: Shorts recommendations. The study provides a matched large-scale comparison between short-form and long-form recommendation behavior, based on 50,000 recommendation pairs from political and nonpolitical seeds. Its practical value is evidence about whether the two formats expose viewers to political content, diversity, engagement, and partisan alignment in different ways. The abstract reports fundamental differences between the algorithms, without giving the exact directions in this input file. That evidence can guide future research on YouTube recommendations and help platform observers ask more precise questions about format-specific political exposure.
375.limits: Several assumptions must hold for the audit to be trusted. The matched short and long videos need to be similar enough that the format comparison is meaningful; if the short version edits the story into a different message, matching is weaker. The labels for political content, diversity, engagement, and partisan alignment must be reliable, but the abstract does not specify how they are assigned. Engagement is only a trace of response, not proof of persuasion or endorsement. The audit observes recommendations from selected seeds, not every user history or personalized setting. Most importantly, the abstract reports differences between algorithms, but it does not prove long-term effects on individual beliefs, voting behavior, or polarization outside the measured recommendation outputs.

376.bp: A person often asks a question whose answer is not just a fact, but a fact at the right time. A weather answer, a traffic decision, or an event-ordering question can be wrong even when every retrieved sentence is true, because the sentence may describe the wrong interval. This paper serves answer systems that use outside evidence with large language models: the model should fetch facts, reason over them, and answer without pretending the world is frozen. The ordinary need is temporal grounding. If a user asks what held before, after, during, or while conditions changed, the system must know when each event happened and when each claim was valid. KG-iRAG treats that need as a structured retrieval problem. It uses a knowledge graph, meaning a linked map of entities, events, and relations, and gives time an explicit role so the answer can be built along a timeline rather than from one static search result.
376.wh: The hard part is that temporal questions mix two jobs that are easy to confuse. The system must find relevant evidence, and it must check whether that evidence fits the requested time relation. A normal retrieval-augmented answer system can fetch passages that mention the right objects, but those passages may describe different moments. One item may be true only during a validity interval, another may describe an event that happened earlier, and a third may be useful only if a later condition also holds. More retrieval can make the problem worse because the answer model receives a larger pile of facts without a disciplined way to order them. Static retrieval also has no memory of what has already been established during a multi-step question. The paper's tension is therefore not simply missing knowledge. It is the danger of composing individually plausible facts into a timeline that contradicts itself, answers too early, or plans with outdated conditions.
376.naive: A smart beginner would connect a search system to a language model, ask for documents related to the question, and let the model write the answer from the retrieved text. If the first answer looks uncertain, the beginner might fetch more documents. That works for questions where relevance is mostly topical, such as finding a definition or a stable fact. It fails for time-dependent questions because the retrieved evidence needs to be placed in order. A document can mention the right city, road, person, or event while belonging to the wrong date or valid interval. The model may then merge old and current facts, treat sequence as a loose hint, or stop after one retrieval even though a later step needs a different piece of evidence.
376.ap: The core idea is to make retrieval loop through time instead of happen once at the beginning. KG-iRAG couples a time-aware planner with a knowledge graph. The planner breaks the question into temporal needs: which event must be before another, which fact must hold during an interval, and which condition must be checked next. The graph stores facts and events with timestamps and validity intervals, so retrieval can be guided by time constraints rather than only by topical similarity. After each retrieval, the system refines an intermediate hypothesis, carries forward the temporal constraints it has learned, and asks for the next piece of evidence that would test or extend that hypothesis. The important move is constraint-guided iteration: each step narrows the search by what must still be temporally consistent, reducing unnecessary retrieval and making the answer a chain of checked deductions.
376.mech: The mechanism starts with a question that requires both knowledge and inference over time. The input may ask for an ordering of events, a fact that was valid during a particular interval, or an action plan under evolving conditions. First, KG-iRAG represents the relevant world as a knowledge graph: things and events become nodes, and relations become links. Unlike a timeless graph, those events and facts carry explicit timestamps or validity intervals. Second, a time-aware planner identifies the temporal structure of the question. It decides what needs to be known first, what time relation must be preserved, and what constraint should guide the next retrieval. Third, retrieval is iterative. The system fetches graph evidence, applies temporal operators that propagate constraints, and updates its working hypothesis. In plain terms, if one retrieved fact says an event happened during a certain period, the next search is not free to ignore that period; it must look for evidence compatible with it. Fourth, the system verifies temporal consistency while composing evidence. Facts that fit the topic but violate the timeline should be rejected or force revision. The output is an answer supported by a step-by-step chain whose pieces have been checked against their timestamps, intervals, and ordering.
376.math: The main mathematical object is a time-stamped graph. A graph is a set of objects connected by relations; here the objects include events and facts, and the relations are useful only when their time conditions make sense. Time adds an ordered axis. That means the system can compare before and after, overlap and non-overlap, still-valid and expired. The second idea is constraint propagation, which is ordinary bookkeeping made precise: once one step establishes a time condition, later steps inherit it instead of starting from a blank search. Operators are rules for moving those conditions through the graph, such as following a relation while preserving an interval or checking that two events can coexist in the requested order. The third idea is iterative search under uncertainty. The system does not know all needed evidence at the start, so it retrieves, scores, checks, and retrieves again. Calibration matters because the abstract claims better alignment between confidence and correctness; in everyday terms, the system should sound less sure when the temporal evidence is thin or inconsistent. The key tradeoff is completeness versus cost: fetch enough to prove the timeline, but avoid reading facts that the current constraints already make irrelevant.
376.dots: This paper sits at the crossing of retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge graphs, information retrieval, and sequence reasoning in the repo's current map. Like the RAG family, it treats outside evidence as necessary but dangerous: retrieved material helps only if the system can decide which pieces deserve trust. Like the knowledge-graph family, it uses linked facts so evidence can be followed through relations rather than searched as isolated text. Its special pressure comes from the time-series and spatiotemporal family: order, intervals, and changing conditions are part of the answer, not metadata that can be ignored. It also connects to multi-answer temporal reasoning papers in the repo, where models fail by stopping too early or by missing valid states across time. KG-iRAG answers a neighboring failure: a model may retrieve once and compose facts fluently, but the composition is unreliable unless every step still fits the timeline.
376.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because time is a strong filter. A normal retriever asks whether evidence is about the right topic. KG-iRAG also asks whether it belongs in the right temporal slot. That extra check removes a common source of wrong answers: facts that are locally relevant but globally inconsistent. Iteration helps because temporal reasoning is often sequential. The system may not know the second retrieval need until the first piece of evidence fixes an interval or event order. Carrying constraints forward means each step uses what was already learned instead of repeatedly searching from the original vague question. The graph helps because relations tell the system where evidence can travel: from an event to its time, from a fact to the interval where it holds, from one condition to another linked condition. The abstract's claims about higher accuracy, better calibration, and reduced unnecessary retrieval fit this mechanism. Better answers come from rejecting timeline-breaking evidence; lower retrieval comes from not fetching branches that constraints rule out.
376.po: The payoff is a retrieval-augmented answer system that can handle questions where timing changes correctness. The paper reports stronger accuracy and calibration than strong RAG baselines on public temporal question-answering benchmarks, while also reducing unnecessary retrieval through targeted, constraint-guided steps. It also builds three application-oriented datasets for real-time decision queries around weather and traffic. Grounded in the abstract, the practical capability is not merely a more fluent answer. It is step-by-step deduction over facts that have timestamps, validity intervals, and temporal relations, so the system can answer or plan when conditions evolve.
376.limits: The method assumes the knowledge graph contains useful facts with reliable timestamps and validity intervals. If the graph is incomplete, stale, wrongly linked, or missing the critical event, constraint-guided retrieval can still produce a confident but incomplete path. The abstract does not show how KG-iRAG handles adversarial evidence, ambiguous time expressions, contradictory sources outside the graph, or domains where validity intervals are fuzzy rather than explicit. Its public benchmarks and three weather or traffic datasets support the claimed setting, but they do not prove that the same temporal operators cover every real-time decision task. The system also depends on the planner correctly decomposing the question; a bad plan can guide retrieval away from the needed evidence.

377.bp: Marketing teams often have to decide where scarce attention and money should go: which customers deserve retention offers, which users should be bid for more aggressively, and which accounts may become worth special treatment. Customer lifetime value prediction tries to estimate the money a customer may bring over the whole relationship, not just the next purchase. The hard part is that the customer base is not shaped like a neat crowd around an average. The abstract says many users have zero value, most remaining users sit in low-to-medium ranges, and a small high-value group carries unusual business importance. CC-OR-Net serves this setting by treating customer value as both an ordering problem and an amount-estimation problem. A useful system must first keep the top-value users from being buried, then still explain differences inside ordinary customer groups where the values are not identical.
377.wh: The central difficulty is that two kinds of imbalance happen at once. First, the low-to-medium users are so numerous that a model trained to reduce average numerical error can spend most of its effort serving them. That can make the final score look good while missing the customers who matter most commercially. Second, the lower and middle range is not simple either: the abstract says there is significant value heterogeneity inside that large user base, so treating all non-whales as one bland mass throws away useful distinctions. Existing approaches face a tradeoff. Rigid statistical assumptions can make the data fit a convenient curve even when the real customer population has many zeros and a long right tail. Ordered buckets can separate tiers, but if the ordering is only encouraged by a training penalty, the model may still learn pieces that fight each other instead of respecting the value order by construction.
377.naive: A smart beginner might collect each customer's past behavior and train one model to predict a single future dollar amount. The model would be rewarded when its predicted number is close to the observed value, averaged across all users. That seems natural because lifetime value is a number. It fails because the average training signal mostly comes from the crowd of low-to-medium users and the many zeros. The rare high-value customers contribute too few cases to steer the model strongly, even though business decisions care about them greatly. Another beginner move is to divide customers into value buckets and train a separate amount predictor, but bucket order can become a soft hope rather than a built-in rule.
377.ap: The paper's central move is structural decoupling: make the architecture itself split the work into ordered value placement and within-tier correction. CC-OR-Net uses a structural ordinal decomposition module for ranking, which means it first organizes customers into value levels whose order is guaranteed by how the model is built. Then an intra-bucket residual module handles fine-grained regression, meaning it predicts the leftover amount differences among customers placed in the same broad value region. Finally, a targeted high-value augmentation module gives extra modeling attention to the top-tier users, where ordinary averaging would under-serve the small but important group. The important design choice is that ordering is not merely punished when violated; it is baked into the model's shape. This lets ranking and amount estimation specialize without pretending they are the same task.
377.mech: The input is a large set of user records from which customer lifetime value must be predicted. The abstract does not list the features, so the safe claim is that each user is represented by whatever behavior or customer information the dataset provides, and the target is future value. CC-OR-Net first passes the user through a structural ordinal decomposition module. This part asks a coarse question: where does this customer sit in an ordered ladder of value? The ladder matters because a top-tier user must outrank a middle-tier user, and a middle-tier user must outrank a low-tier user. Instead of asking a loss function to clean up ordering mistakes afterward, the model structure is arranged so the ranking relation is guaranteed. Next, the intra-bucket residual module works inside the chosen or implied bucket. It does not have to explain the whole long-tail range at once; it estimates the remaining difference among users within a narrower value zone. Finally, the targeted high-value augmentation module focuses on top-tier customers, adding extra signal for the rare whale segment. The output is a lifetime value estimate that combines coarse ordered placement, fine within-bucket adjustment, and special care for the highest-value users.
377.math: The main mathematical idea is ordered prediction. Instead of treating value levels as unrelated labels, the model uses the fact that the labels have a natural direction: low comes before medium, and medium comes before high. Ordinal decomposition means breaking one hard numerical task into ordered yes-or-no or tier questions whose answers must fit that direction. This fits lifetime value because a marketing decision often first needs relative priority: who should be above whom? The second idea is residual prediction, which means predicting what is left after a coarse explanation has done its job. If a bucket says two users are both medium-value, the residual part estimates the smaller difference between them rather than re-solving the whole problem from zero. The third idea is balancing competing errors. A single average error can favor the majority and neglect rare whales; targeted augmentation changes the training emphasis so rare high-value cases are not numerically drowned out. The tradeoff is global accuracy versus high-value precision across customer tiers. CC-OR-Net's architecture tries to hold both by separating ordering, local amount correction, and top-tier emphasis.
377.dots: This paper connects to the repo's recurring ranking idea because it turns a huge customer pile into an ordered priority list where only a small top group may receive expensive action. It also connects to probability and prediction work because future customer value is uncertain, delayed, sparse, and unevenly observed. The nearby DynaMoLTV paper for online games has the same pressure in a different market: many users spend nothing, a few become whales, and the model must identify high-value users without losing overall value accuracy. The video-ranking LTV paper has a related long-term decision problem, but there the difficulty includes position bias, attribution ambiguity, and time windows in a feed. The revenue A/B testing paper in the repo shows the measurement version of the same shape: whales can dominate money outcomes and make averages noisy. CC-OR-Net belongs to this broader family because it asks how to keep rare, economically important cases visible while still modeling the ordinary majority.
377.ww: The mechanism should help because it reduces a clash between tasks that pull a single model in different directions. Ranking asks for correct order: put more valuable customers above less valuable customers. Regression asks for numerical closeness: predict the amount. In long-tail data, these goals are not identical. A model can be close on many small users while misplacing a whale, or it can chase whales and become sloppy on common users. By giving the ordered ranking job its own structural module, CC-OR-Net protects the coarse value ladder. By giving within-bucket differences to a residual module, it makes the amount-estimation problem smaller and more local. By adding targeted high-value augmentation, it gives the rare top group more influence than its raw count would allow. The result is not magic; it works when the value ladder is a useful simplification of the customer base and when within-tier corrections capture real remaining differences. Under those conditions, the architecture matches the shape of the business problem.
377.po: The payoff is a lifetime value predictor designed for commercial use rather than only average numerical neatness. The abstract says CC-OR-Net was evaluated on real-world datasets with more than 300 million users and achieved a better tradeoff across key business metrics than prior methods, including stronger handling of high-value precision while preserving global accuracy. In practical terms, this can support decisions that need both breadth and focus: ordinary customers should not be ignored, but rare high-value users should not disappear inside the majority. The method buys a cleaner separation between customer ordering and exact value estimation.
377.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The customer value tiers must be meaningful enough that an ordered decomposition helps rather than forcing artificial boundaries. The input data must contain signals that distinguish future high-value users from ordinary users; architecture cannot recover information that is absent. The high-value augmentation must emphasize whales without overfitting quirks of a few unusual customers. The abstract reports large real-world datasets and better business metrics, but it does not show which features were used, how the buckets are defined, how performance varies across industries, or how the method behaves when customer behavior changes after marketing policies change.

378.bp: A search engine is supposed to be a way of sampling the web for independent evidence. A person asks a question, the system sorts a huge pile of pages, and the top results become the facts that downstream tools and readers see. This paper asks what happens when a growing share of that pile is not original human evidence but AI-written text, especially text produced by large language models, systems that generate fluent answers from learned text patterns. The risk is not just that some pages are bad. The deeper risk is circular: web search retrieves AI-written pages, retrieval-augmented generation systems use those pages as evidence, and new AI-written pages then echo the same material back into the web. The paper calls this Retrieval Collapse: first, synthetic sources take over exposure and reduce source diversity; then low-quality or adversarial sources enter the retrieval pipeline.
378.wh: The hard part is that failure can look like success from the outside. Ordinary spam often has visible clues: strange wording, irrelevant keywords, or obvious manipulation. High-quality SEO-style AI content can instead be fluent, topical, and good enough to preserve answer accuracy in the short term. That creates a deceptively healthy state: the answer may still be right, while the evidence base has quietly narrowed to recycled synthetic sources. The abstract reports exactly this kind of mismatch: when the candidate pool was 67% contaminated, exposure contamination rose above 80%, yet answer accuracy remained stable. A second difficulty is adversarial contamination. A bad actor can craft content that seems relevant to the search system while carrying harmful or manipulative instructions. Retrieval systems therefore face two tensions at once: preserving diverse original sources and suppressing dangerous sources without simply rejecting every AI-looking page.
378.naive: A smart beginner might say: just rank pages by relevance, then check whether the final answer is accurate. If the answer remains correct, the system is fine. This fails because relevance and provenance are different questions. A synthetic page can match the query and repeat a true claim while still replacing independent evidence with recycled text. Accuracy also misses delayed damage: once synthetic pages dominate exposure, future systems train on and retrieve from a thinner, less diverse web. Another beginner fix is to use a standard keyword ranker such as BM25, which scores documents by matching query words against document words. But keyword matching cannot reliably tell helpful synthetic text from adversarial synthetic text.
378.ap: The paper's central move is to treat retrieval pollution as an ecosystem process, not as a one-document quality problem. It separates the collapse into two stages. In the first stage, AI-generated content becomes common enough in the searchable pool that the top results are disproportionately synthetic, reducing the variety of sources users and RAG systems see. In the second stage, low-quality or adversarial content enters the same pipeline and can influence the evidence shown to a model or user. The experiments make these stages visible by controlling the kind and amount of contamination. One setting uses high-quality SEO-style synthetic content, the kind that can look useful and harmless. Another uses adversarially crafted content, where the question is whether rankers can keep harmful material out. The comparison includes BM25 and LLM-based rankers, which use a language model to judge or reorder candidates.
378.mech: The mechanism starts with a retrieval pool: a set of candidate web pages or page-like documents that a search system could return for a query. The experiment changes the makeup of that pool by adding controlled amounts of AI-generated material. In the SEO-style setting, the synthetic material is designed to be relevant and polished, so the test is not merely whether the search engine can spot junk. The system then ranks candidates and exposes a small top portion to users or to a RAG pipeline. The key measurement is not only pool contamination, meaning the share of synthetic material available, but exposure contamination, meaning the share of synthetic material that actually appears in the results people or models consume. The abstract reports a sharp amplification: 67% contamination in the pool produced more than 80% contamination in exposure. The paper also keeps track of answer accuracy, showing that surface correctness can remain stable even when evidence diversity erodes. In the adversarial setting, the input includes harmful crafted content. Different rankers then score or reorder the candidates. BM25, a word-overlap scoring rule, exposed about 19% harmful content, while LLM-based rankers suppressed it more strongly.
378.math: The main mathematics is ranking under contamination. Ranking means turning many candidate documents into an ordered list by assigning each candidate a score for the current query. BM25 is a classic scoring rule: it counts useful word matches while correcting for words that are common everywhere and for document length. This is a good first language for search because many information needs are partly expressed by shared words, but it is blind to source origin and intent unless those facts affect the words. The paper also uses the mathematics of proportions and exposure. Pool contamination is a fraction of the available evidence; exposure contamination is a fraction of what the ranking system actually shows. Comparing those two fractions reveals amplification: the ranking process can make a polluted pool look even more polluted at the top. In adversarial tests, the mathematical object is a decision boundary: harmful versus acceptable content after scoring. LLM-based rankers add a richer scoring function, where a language model evaluates meaning and likely harm rather than only word overlap. The tradeoff is speed and simplicity versus deeper judgment, and relevance versus source diversity.
378.dots: This paper connects directly to the repository's Information Retrieval & Search family, where 465 papers are grouped around choosing useful evidence from huge collections, and to the Retrieval-Augmented RAG family, where 182 papers study systems that retrieve documents before generating answers. It is closest to the robustness branch: the family data includes Conflict-Aware RAG, OpenDecoder, poisoning and attack papers, and multimodal RAG security work. Those papers share a hidden problem with this one: retrieval is no longer just finding something relevant; it must decide which evidence deserves to enter an answer-making pipeline. The paper also links to ranking, because top positions define what evidence counts; to probability, because contamination rates estimate ecosystem risk from repeated trials; and to misinformation or trust, because synthetic content can be plausible without being independent. Its special contribution is to frame pollution as a self-reinforcing web-level cycle.
378.ww: The approach works because it measures the failure at the place where harm appears: the exposed evidence, not only the raw web pool or the final answer. If synthetic pages are 67% of the pool but more than 80% of the shown results, then ranking is not a neutral window into the web; it is concentrating the pollution. That observation would be invisible if one only checked answer accuracy. The split between SEO-style and adversarial content is also important. Polished synthetic content tests whether systems can preserve source diversity when badness is subtle. Adversarial content tests whether systems can keep deliberately harmful material out. Comparing BM25 with LLM-based rankers then explains why richer judgment can help: word overlap sees topical match, while a language model ranker can use broader cues about meaning and harmful intent. The result is not that language model rankers solve collapse. It is that different failure modes require different defenses: provenance and diversity controls for quiet homogenization, stronger semantic screening for adversarial infiltration.
378.po: The payoff is a clearer warning signal for web-grounded systems. The paper shows that a retrieval pipeline can become heavily dependent on synthetic evidence while ordinary answer accuracy still looks stable. It also quantifies two concrete risks from the abstract: more than 80% exposure contamination under a 67% contaminated SEO-style pool, and about 19% harmful exposure for BM25 under adversarial contamination. LLM-based rankers suppress adversarial content more strongly, suggesting that ranker design matters. The practical capability is diagnostic: builders can evaluate whether their retrieval stack is preserving source diversity and resisting harmful infiltration, instead of only asking whether answers look correct today.
378.limits: The abstract supports strong claims about controlled experiments, not a complete measurement of the entire live web. The results depend on how the SEO-style and adversarial content were created, which queries were used, which rankers were tested, and how exposure and harm were labeled. Stable answer accuracy in the experiment does not prove long-term safety; it is part of the warning, because short-term correctness can hide source collapse. LLM-based rankers suppress adversarial content better in the reported setting, but the abstract does not prove they will catch adaptive attacks or preserve diversity. The paper also assumes that synthetic provenance and source diversity are important for trustworthy retrieval, an assumption that is plausible but still needs system-specific policy choices.

379.bp: The real object in this tutorial is a web system that no longer only returns pages or writes answers. It acts: a language model can choose what text to generate, which content to show, which recommendation strategy to try, which other agent to coordinate with, and how to adjust after users or partner agents respond. That turns the web into a continuing decision environment. A fixed language model is like a clerk with a script: useful for familiar requests, but weak when the right move depends on live feedback. The tutorial argues that multi-armed bandits fit this setting because they treat each possible action as an option whose value is partly unknown. The need comes before the method: agentic language systems must keep serving users while learning which choices work. They cannot pause the world to test every possible response, content item, or interaction style.
379.wh: The hard part is that every action has two jobs at once. It should be useful now, and it should teach the system something useful for later. If an agent always picks the response, article, tool path, or recommendation style that has worked best so far, it may miss a better option that has not yet had enough trials. If it experiments too freely, real users receive worse answers or irrelevant content while the system learns. The abstract also places the problem in a networked multi-agent setting, where one agent's behavior can affect another agent's response. That makes feedback less clean than a laboratory label. A reward may reflect the generated text, the user's taste, another agent's strategy, timing, or a platform goal. The system must learn under uncertainty while staying fast enough for web scale and stable enough for autonomous operation.
379.naive: A smart beginner would choose a few rules by hand: always use the highest-rated generation style, always recommend the category with the most clicks, or let each language-model agent follow the same fixed prompt and update it occasionally from aggregate results. This fails because early evidence can be misleading. The first winning option may simply have been shown to easier users or tried at a lucky time. A rule also wastes the chance to learn from uncertain alternatives. In personalized content and recommendation, different users may reward different choices, so one global winner can become a trap. In multi-agent dialogue, a fixed behavior can stop adapting when other agents change.
379.ap: The central move is to put a small decision engine around the language model. Instead of treating generation or recommendation as one fixed path, the system lists possible actions as arms: alternative text-generation choices, content-selection policies, interaction strategies, or recommendation moves. After choosing one, it observes a reward, meaning some measurable sign that the choice helped, such as better interaction quality, stronger content fit, or a successful recommendation outcome. The agent then updates its belief about that option while keeping some room to test other options. The tutorial covers familiar bandit strategies such as epsilon-greedy, UCB, and Thompson Sampling. In plain terms, these are different ways to decide when to trust the current favorite and when to try an uncertain option because the missing knowledge may be worth the temporary risk.
379.mech: The mechanism starts with a situation: a user request, a content feed moment, a dialogue turn between agents, or a recommendation opportunity. The language model or agentic platform has a set of candidate moves. Each candidate is treated as an arm, not because it is literally a slot-machine handle, but because pulling it means trying that action and receiving feedback afterward. The system chooses an arm using an exploration policy. In epsilon-greedy, most choices follow the currently best-known arm, while a small share deliberately tests another arm. In UCB, an arm gets credit both for high observed reward and for uncertainty, so options with little evidence can still be tried. In Thompson Sampling, the system samples from its current belief about each arm and lets uncertainty naturally produce experiments. After the action, the system records a reward signal. The reward design is crucial: it must translate messy outcomes such as dialogue coordination, content relevance, or recommendation success into a number or comparable signal. The bandit updater then changes the estimated value of the chosen arm. Over many interactions, weak arms are chosen less often, useful arms are chosen more often, and uncertain arms still receive enough trials to avoid premature lock-in. The output is not just text; it is an adaptive policy for future web actions.
379.math: The main mathematical idea is decision-making under uncertainty. A multi-armed bandit is a repeated-choice problem where each option has an unknown payoff, and the learner only observes the payoff of the option it actually tried. That limited feedback matters here because an agent does not know what would have happened if it had generated a different response or shown a different item. Probability enters as measured belief: the system estimates how likely each action is to produce useful feedback based on past trials, while admitting that thin evidence should not be treated as certainty. The exploration-exploitation trade-off is the central pressure. Exploitation means using the option that currently looks best; exploration means spending some decisions to learn about options whose value is still unclear. UCB adds an uncertainty bonus, which is a way of saying that an option with few observations deserves a chance before being dismissed. Thompson Sampling turns uncertain belief into randomized choice, so less-certain options are tried in proportion to how plausible their success still is. Optimization, in this paper's sense, means repeatedly adjusting the action-choice rule to improve the reward signal. The risk is that the reward number compresses many human and platform goals into one target.
379.dots: This tutorial sits at the crossing of several recurring conference ideas. It belongs with LLM agents and tool-use work because the language model is being treated as a worker that chooses actions, coordinates with other agents, and adapts from outcomes rather than only producing one answer. It belongs with recommender-systems work because content selection and recommendation are short-listing problems: many possible items or strategies compete for a small amount of user attention. It belongs with reinforcement-learning work because the system acts, observes feedback, and changes future behavior, although the bandit setting is narrower because it focuses on repeated choices with limited feedback rather than full long-horizon planning. It also connects to probability and ranking. Probability keeps uncertainty visible when evidence is partial, while ranking appears whenever arms are ordered by expected usefulness. The common field-level problem is controlled attention: decide what to try next when acting teaches the system but can also cost users, money, time, or trust.
379.ww: The approach should help because agentic web systems contain repeated decision points with feedback. A language model does not have to solve every future case from first principles if past interactions reveal that certain generation choices, content policies, or recommendation strategies often work in similar settings. Bandits improve on the naive fixed rule by refusing to confuse current evidence with final truth. An option that has done well receives more use, so the system benefits from what it has learned. An option that has little evidence can still be tested, so the system can discover better behavior after user needs, available content, or other agents change. This is especially natural for web-scale systems, where the same kind of choice recurs many times and small updates can accumulate into better routing of attention. The mechanism also fits decentralized agentic settings because each agent can adapt from its own observed rewards without requiring a single complete model of the whole web. The benefit depends on feedback being frequent and meaningful enough to guide learning.
379.po: The payoff is an agentic language platform that can keep adapting instead of relying only on fixed prompts or offline training. The tutorial's examples point to three capabilities: coordinating multi-agent dialogue, dynamically curating personalized content, and improving recommendation strategies. In each case, the bandit layer gives the system a disciplined way to try alternatives, learn from response signals, and gradually favor actions that work better in practice. The result is not a guarantee of perfect autonomy; it is a practical control loop for systems that must make many small web decisions while evidence is still incomplete.
379.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The system needs a reward signal that truly reflects the desired outcome; clicks, engagement, or short-term satisfaction can mislead if they ignore quality, safety, diversity, or long-term trust. The set of arms must be defined well enough that useful alternatives are available to test. Feedback must arrive often enough for learning, and past interactions must remain relevant as users, content, and other agents change. The abstract names case studies but does not prove which reward designs, exploration policies, or scaling choices are safest across all agentic web deployments.

380.bp: Online advertising is a fast marketplace run by predictions. For every ad opportunity, ranking and delivery systems estimate which ad should be shown and what that opportunity is worth. Those numbers do not stay inside a model; they affect pricing, delivery, advertiser spend, and the platform's business logic. Prediction Guardian serves the moment when the model still returns numbers, but the numbers have quietly stopped behaving like healthy ad predictions. The paper points to several sources of this danger: large recommendation models are retrained often on fresh data from many sources, new versions are deployed continuously as user behavior changes, and real-time feature pipelines can send bad inputs during serving. A crash is easy to notice. A prediction stream that is slightly too high, slightly too low, or full of extreme values is harder, because it can look operationally normal while pushing wrong prices downstream.
380.wh: The hard part is that a single prediction cannot usually be judged in isolation. One ad might naturally receive a high value because the user, page, advertiser, and timing make it promising. Another might receive a low value for ordinary reasons. If the system simply checks whether each score is above or below a handpicked limit, it will confuse rare but legitimate cases with failures, and it will miss broad shifts where every score moves only a little. The abstract also says the risks come from both training and serving. Corrupted training data can teach a model a bad pattern before deployment, while upstream feature issues can damage the information arriving at inference time. Either way, the model may continue producing plausible-looking numbers. The platform needs to notice shape changes in the whole stream quickly enough to prevent pricing harm, without requiring labels that say which individual ad prediction was wrong.
380.naive: A smart beginner would start with alarms on individual predictions: flag any score that is too large, too small, or different from yesterday's average. That catches obvious spikes, but it is too crude for ad ranking. Healthy advertising predictions often have a long tail: many ordinary low or moderate values and a smaller number of large values. A real high-value ad is not automatically an error. The beginner might also wait for downstream pricing reports, but by then bad predictions have already affected delivery. Another simple plan is frequent retraining, yet the abstract names retraining itself as part of the exposure, because fresh multi-source data can be silently corrupted. The failure is treating the problem as a bad-number problem when it is really a bad-pattern problem.
380.ap: Prediction Guardian's central move is to watch the population of prediction scores rather than arguing with each score one by one. In a healthy system, the abstract says aggregate prediction distributions typically have log-normal characteristics: most values live in the lower or middle range, while a thinner tail stretches toward larger values. The system keeps historical baselines for that normal shape and continuously compares the real-time prediction stream against them. When the current shape moves left, moves right, or grows an unusual tail, the system treats that as evidence that training corruption, serving features, or model behavior may have shifted. The same monitoring layer also acts after detection. It applies targeted mitigation, including selective smoothing and zeroing out outliers, so the suspicious part of the prediction stream is damped before it can produce downstream pricing inaccuracies.
380.mech: The mechanism starts with the ad system's real-time outputs: the predicted values produced by deep learning recommendation models used for ranking and delivery. Instead of inspecting only individual requests, Prediction Guardian groups many recent predictions into an aggregate distribution, a picture of how often different score ranges appear. It then compares that current picture with historical baselines taken from healthy operation. The abstract names Jensen-Shannon divergence as one of the comparison measures. In plain terms, this asks how much the current score pattern and the expected score pattern disagree, while keeping the comparison stable enough to use in monitoring. If the disagreement passes the system's anomaly standard, the detector classifies the kind of movement it sees. A leftward shift means many predictions have moved lower, which can lead to underprediction. A rightward shift means predictions are generally higher, which can cause over-pricing or over-delivery. A tail elevation means too many extreme values appear in the high end. After detection, mitigation is targeted to the shape of the problem. Smoothing reduces suspicious irregular values instead of letting them pass unchanged. Zeroing out outliers removes values judged too dangerous to use. The output is not a repaired model; it is a stabilized prediction stream for downstream pricing and ranking.
380.math: The main mathematical object is a distribution, meaning a count-based shape that says how a large batch of prediction values is spread across possible ranges. This fits the paper because advertising prediction errors can be collective. A model can be wrong not because one value is strange, but because the whole stream has shifted. The log-normal idea gives a baseline shape: values are positive, many are modest, and a smaller tail contains large predictions. The comparison idea is measured surprise. Jensen-Shannon divergence measures how different two distributions are by asking how much information is gained when one learns which distribution a value came from. If today's scores look like the historical healthy shape, the surprise is small. If the stream has moved left, moved right, or swollen at the tail, the surprise rises. Mitigation then uses a second mathematical instinct: reduce harmful error in the values passed downstream. Smoothing replaces a suspicious sharp value with a less extreme one, trading some detail for stability. Zeroing an outlier is a stronger rule that sacrifices that prediction entirely to avoid greater pricing harm. The tradeoff is sensitivity versus false alarms: react too slowly and corruption spreads; react too eagerly and legitimate market changes get suppressed.
380.dots: This paper sits at the crossing of anomaly detection, ranking, probability, and advertising systems. Like other anomaly-detection work in the repo's family data, it repairs a weak definition of normal by comparing current behavior with an expected pattern. Its surface object is not a wallet, log stream, graph, or user account, but the same deeper question appears: when has a live system stopped fitting the world it claims to represent? It also connects to ranking because ad delivery depends on ordered choices made from scores; if the scores shift, the order and prices can shift too. It connects to probability because the detector acts before it knows the true outcome of each ad opportunity, using repeated prediction patterns as evidence. Within the advertising and e-commerce family, it belongs to the trust branch: commercial systems need guards that catch silent corruption, evasion, inappropriate behavior, or hidden costs before marketplace decisions amplify them.
380.ww: The approach works when failures leave fingerprints in the aggregate prediction stream. Silent corruption in training data or upstream features may not identify itself with an error message, but it can make many predictions lower, higher, or more extreme than healthy history would suggest. Looking at the distribution gives the detector more evidence than any one ad request can provide. A single unusual score may be legitimate; a systematic shape change across many scores is harder to dismiss. The method also fits the speed requirement. It does not need to wait for conversions, refunds, advertiser complaints, or manual labels. It can compare recent predictions with baselines as the system runs, then apply a bounded intervention to the suspicious region. Selective smoothing helps when values are distorted but still contain some useful signal. Zeroing outliers helps when extreme values are more dangerous than informative. The gain over the naive approach is that the system watches the health of the score-generating process, not just isolated score thresholds.
380.po: The abstract reports that Prediction Guardian was tested on three corruption shapes: leftward shifts that cause underprediction, rightward shifts that cause over-prediction, and tail elevation shifts that create too many extreme values. It reports anomaly detection above 0.80 precision and above 0.85 recall with 16.7-minute average latency in simulation, and 0.75 precision with above 0.85 recall and 18.3-minute average latency in historical backtesting. The mitigation result is also concrete: advertiser pricing accuracy improves by over 90% for tail outliers and over 50% for moderate right-shift anomalies. The practical payoff is a real-time guardrail for ad prediction streams.
380.limits: The paper's claims depend on healthy prediction streams having stable enough historical shapes to compare against, including the stated log-normal characteristics. If user behavior or advertiser demand changes legitimately, a detector could mistake real market movement for corruption. If corruption is subtle enough to preserve the aggregate distribution while damaging important subgroups, distribution monitoring may miss it. The abstract does not prove that smoothing or zeroing is always the right mitigation, only that the proposed method helped in the tested corruption scenarios. It also reports simulation and historical backtesting, not every possible live deployment condition, upstream failure, model version, advertiser segment, or adversarial attempt to hide inside the expected distribution.

381.bp: Online communities in Chinese-language spaces are flooded with toxic speech in obfuscated forms—deliberately misspelled, symbolized, or hidden in phonetic encodings to evade detection. Cleaning up toxic content at scale requires understanding these variants, but manually coding every permutation is impossible.
381.wh: Toxic language detection is normally pattern-matching: look for known bad words. But bad actors deliberately mutate words—using pinyin abbreviations, replacing characters with visually similar ones, mixing in symbols. A static rulebook can't keep up with the creativity of evasion. You need a system that understands how variants relate to canonical toxic terms.
381.ap: This work builds a knowledge graph that maps canonical toxic terms to their variants using three types of relationships: phonetic similarity (sounds like the real word), visual resemblance (looks like the real word), and contextual co-occurrence (appears together with known toxic content). A small labeled dataset fine-tunes an LLM for initial normalization. Then during detection, the system uses the graph to reason about whether a variant is likely toxic, and fills in missing graph connections on the fly.
381.ww: The knowledge graph structure lets the system generalize from known variants to unseen ones. If it knows 'xyz' and 'abc' are both variants of the same toxic term, and sees a new combination 'xyzabc' for the first time, it can infer this is also toxic by following the graph. The LLM reasoning handles incomplete knowledge by inferring likely paths.
381.po: Tested on multiple Chinese toxic language datasets, this approach consistently beats static detection and outperforms other knowledge-enhanced systems. It catches obfuscated variants better than prior work, making it practical for scaling content moderation in Chinese online environments.

382.bp: Dengue fever outbreaks devastate tropical cities; early warning saves lives. Tainan City has suffered multiple dengue surges, yet traditional forecasting methods are too slow or too coarse-grained. If public health officials had accurate, weekly, village-level predictions, they could deploy resources exactly where the next outbreak will hit.
382.wh: Epidemic forecasting is complex: disease spread depends on mosquito populations (entomological data), human behavior, climate, population density, neighborhood connectivity. All of these change over time and space. Simple models either ignore spatial structure (treating the whole city as one pool) or can't update quickly enough to catch emerging hotspots.
382.ap: G-SEIR combines a learnable SEIR epidemiological simulator with a spatio-temporal graph neural network. SEIR is a compartmental model that tracks susceptible, exposed, infected, and recovered populations. But instead of fixed parameters, the system learns how to weight transitions between compartments. The graph neural network captures how disease spreads between districts and villages by treating them as nodes with edges representing movement and contact.
382.ww: By learning rather than hand-tuning epidemic parameters, the system adapts to real outbreak dynamics. The graph structure lets information flow between neighboring regions—if a district sees rising cases, the model knows adjacent villages are at higher risk. Combining epidemiology (which captures disease biology) with learning (which captures local variation) avoids both unrealistic assumptions and pure curve-fitting.
382.po: On Tainan's 2015 and 2023 outbreaks, G-SEIR outperforms eleven baselines on prediction accuracy. It generates fine-grained, weekly forecasts for 752 villages—granular enough for authorities to target interventions. A web interface lets officials spot emerging hotspots in real time, supporting proactive disease control instead of reactive response.

383.bp: Fashion-conscious shoppers searching for clothing online want to find items matching specific attributes—a red leather jacket, blue denim with distressing, etc. Text search fails (most people can't describe finesse), so image search is essential. But finding items with subtle attribute combinations is hard because backgrounds, lighting, and pose clutter the signal.
383.wh: Patch-based attention methods slice images into grids and focus on relevant patches. But fashion attributes like 'distressed denim' or 'leather sleeve detail' don't align neatly with rectangular grids—they sprawl across irregular regions and get drowned out by background. Simply looking harder at the right patches isn't enough; you need tokens that capture semantic regions naturally.
383.ap: This work (Super Fashion) uses superpixels instead of patches. Superpixels are chunks of the image with similar color and texture, forming semantically coherent regions (a sleeveless armhole, a plaid pattern, a metal zipper). First, an attribute-guided attention mechanism identifies which regions matter for the target attribute. Then superpixel segmentation groups pixels within those regions into compact tokens. A Transformer fuses superpixel tokens with attribute tokens, letting the model learn both what to look for and where to find it.
383.ww: Superpixels follow image structure better than grids do. A leather texture naturally forms a superpixel; a plaid pattern does too. By using these natural regions as tokens, the model can focus on semantically meaningful units rather than fighting with grid-aligned noise. Attribute-guided attention narrows the focus first, so superpixel segmentation works on clean, relevant regions.
383.po: On fashion retrieval benchmarks (FashionAI, DARN, DeepFashion), Super Fashion improves ranking accuracy by 1.84%-9.35% over prior methods. It finds items with matching attributes more reliably, making fashion search more useful for people with specific style preferences.

384.bp: Training machine learning models requires millions of human labels—images annotated as safe or unsafe, text classified as harmful or clean. Crowdsourcing these labels is cheap at scale, but workers vary wildly in honesty and skill. Some contribute high-quality labels; others game the system or submit garbage. Current incentive schemes can't separate good from bad contributors.
384.wh: Paying everyone equally encourages fraud. Someone labeling random answers gets paid the same as someone laboring carefully. Paying more risky rewards bad contributors proportionally to their damage (they earn money for sabotaging), and discourages participation. You need a system that rewards honesty, punishes fraud, without killing willingness to participate.
384.ap: This work (NAI) applies signed Shapley values to crowdsourcing. Shapley value is a game-theory tool for apportioning credit fairly; NAI extends it to assign negative credit for harmful contributions. It estimates each worker's ability (skill level), combines it with real-time task results to score their contribution (positive or negative), then uses a dynamic stake pool—a kind of escrow where workers post collateral. If their contribution is positive, they recoup and earn. If negative, they lose part of their stake.
384.ww: The Shapley approach distributes credit precisely: it accounts for what each worker contributed relative to the rest of the team. A worker who submitted a bad label when others agreed loses credit; one who rescued a mislabeled image gains it. The stake pool creates cost for bad behavior without blocking future participation—workers can recover and rebuild trust.
384.po: Deployed on NetEase's crowdsourcing platform with 80,000 monthly active workers, NAI improved labeling accuracy by 59.6% for beginner tasks and reduced fraud rates by 14.8%-33.9% across all difficulty levels. It scales to millions of labels while maintaining quality and trust.

385.bp: Recommendation systems crave data—the more user-item interactions recorded, the better the model learns. But most people interact with only a tiny fraction of items (movies, products, news), leaving the system with vast sparse regions of unknowns. Also, popular items get recommended far more than niche ones, creating imbalance. These two problems cripple recommendation quality.
385.wh: Sparsity and imbalance are baked into user behavior: most people are passive; blockbuster items dominate views. Simple fixes like adding fake interactions make things worse. You can't just generate more data; you have to generate the right data—interactions that fill gaps believably and balance class representation without breaking the underlying recommendation structure.
385.ap: This work reframes the problem using line graphs. Instead of thinking about user-item interactions, it transforms them into a line graph where nodes are interactions and edges connect interactions that share a user or item. Sparsity and class imbalance become a node-classification problem in the line graph (too few labeled nodes, imbalanced labels). The work proposes LGDA: a data augmentation strategy that generates high-quality balanced pseudo-interactions using the line graph structure, then filters them by confidence to keep only believable ones.
385.ww: Line graph structure captures interaction patterns naturally. Two interactions sharing a user are connected; the model can see that generating similar interactions is plausible. By treating it as a node-classification task on the line graph, the work leverages mature imbalanced-learning techniques. Confidence filtering prevents junk augmentation from degrading real interactions.
385.po: On four real-world recommendation datasets, LGDA improves recommendation performance and system robustness without modifying the underlying model. It's a plug-and-play fix for data sparsity and imbalance, letting practitioners boost quality without redesigning their entire system.

386.bp: The field of web technologies spans social networks, graphs, privacy, security, fairness, and ethics. Each area has crucial papers that critically analyze models and methods. TIME is a workshop bringing together domain experts and newcomers to distill key insights from these papers into actionable knowledge.
386.wh: Research literature explodes faster than any individual can read. A newcomer to web security, graph algorithms, or fairness faces hundreds of papers with no clear starting point. Practitioners need quick reference guides, not original research. Critical analysis that compares methods across papers—which approaches work, where they fail, what tradeoffs exist—is rare but invaluable.
386.ap: TIME solicits survey, evaluation, and review papers that take a birds-eye view of a subfield. Papers might compare datasets, analyze trends in methods, or reconcile conflicting findings. The workshop complements these with invited talks from industry experts sharing practical experience. Discussions and networking create space for cross-domain collaboration.
386.ww: Surveys and reviews synthesize what the community has learned, identify blind spots, and point out promising directions. By bringing experts and newcomers together, the workshop bridges research and practice. Talks ground theory in real-world constraints (at a 3B-user platform, this approach broke for X reason). Attendees leave with a map of the field, not just isolated papers.
386.po: Participants gain actionable knowledge for their own work: understanding which privacy techniques scale, how fairness definitions interact with real deployments, which graph algorithms actually work at web scale. The workshop becomes a trusted resource for anyone starting work in web technologies.

387.bp: Industrial control systems (ICS)—power grids, water treatment, manufacturing—require safety-critical response times measured in tens of milliseconds. Security researchers often propose blockchain and encryption as panaceas. But if these slow down the control loop to hundreds of milliseconds, the system becomes unsafe. Real security must preserve the ability to respond in time.
387.wh: Blockchain consensus is inherently probabilistic—nodes negotiate agreement, introducing jitter. Homomorphic encryption (allowing computation on encrypted data) requires intensive computation, adding 100+ millisecond overhead. Industrial controllers need <10ms response time to be safe. The math is brutal: 51-440ms latencies violate safety-critical requirements by factors of 5-44x.
387.ap: This work analyzes where encryption overhead is incurred across the Purdue Model of industrial networks (Levels 0-5, from sensors to cloud). It shows BC+HE architectures create a 'dead zone' bottleneck at gateway levels, exposing vulnerabilities. The alternative: use lightweight lattice-based cryptography (LWE, Ring-LWE) for fast sensor-to-controller authentication (meeting <10ms constraints), and reserve BC+HE for non-real-time enterprise layers.
387.ww: Lattice cryptography is computationally cheap and quantum-resistant, making it suitable for real-time layers. Enterprise layers don't need microsecond response; they can absorb blockchain's latency. By decoupling security strategies by layer—speed for critical loops, richness for non-critical enterprise—the system achieves both safety and security without compromise.
387.po: The paper identifies a critical flaw in the BC+HE security paradigm for ICS: it can make systems unsafe. The lattice-based alternative preserves real-time safety while securing the network. This informs how ICS defenders should architect security without sacrificing responsiveness.

388.bp: LLM-enhanced search engines (ChatGPT, Gemini) are changing how people find information. They retrieve web content and synthesize answers, combining search's breadth with LLM reasoning. But attackers have learned SEO tricks over decades. Do these new systems fall for the old attacks, or do they deflect them better?
388.wh: Traditional search engines rank by links and keywords; attackers exploit both. LLM-enhanced search adds a new retrieval phase (finding relevant documents) and a ranking phase (deciding which sources matter). No one has systematically tested whether LLMSEs are vulnerable to known SEO attacks or if the LLM component acts as a defense.
388.ap: This work builds SEO-Bench, a dataset of 1,000 real-world black-hat SEO websites, and tests ten LLMSEs against them. They measure whether traditional SEO attacks (keyword stuffing, cloaking, link manipulation) work. They then propose new LLMSEO attacks: rewritten-query stuffing (rephrasing injection to evade detection) and segmented texts (hiding attacks across multiple retrieved documents). They measure manipulation rates on both.
388.ww: LLMSEs block traditional SEO attacks at the retrieval phase—the filter is strong. But the LLM reasoning phase can be fooled by attacks tailored to it. Rewriting queries to look like legitimate user intent, or fragmenting text so no single document looks suspicious but their union does, exploits the LLM's synthesis step. The system's new power creates new vulnerabilities.
388.po: The paper shows LLMSEs are robust against known SEO but vulnerable to LLMSEO variants—manipulation rates roughly double. This is the first systematic security analysis of LLM search, offering vendors concrete attack patterns to defend against and setting research direction for hardening these systems.

389.bp: Federated learning lets multiple parties train an AI model together without sharing raw data—banks collaborate on fraud detection, hospitals on disease prediction. But if one party wants to use a different model architecture (a smaller model on mobile, a larger one on desktop), the system breaks. Existing methods assume everyone uses the same model.
389.wh: Models are heterogeneous in practice: mobile clients can't run 500M-parameter networks. If a hospital uses a 1B-parameter model and a clinic uses 100M, how do they train together? Naive approaches ask everyone to use the global model, wasting resources on small clients and handicapping large ones. You need a way to federate across different architectures.
389.ap: FedBridge deploys a fusion model on each edge server that learns knowledge from heterogeneous client models via knowledge distillation (training the fusion model to mimic the client model's predictions). It uses a contrastive loss to align fusion model outputs with the global model, handling data heterogeneity. On the cloud server, a block-based aggregation merges fusion models from edge servers into a global model.
389.ww: Knowledge distillation lets a smaller or differently-shaped model pass its learned knowledge to another model without requiring them to share architecture. By intermediate fusion at edge servers, each client's model never needs to match others; they only need to communicate with their local edge fusion model. Block-based aggregation lets the cloud server combine fundamentally different models.
389.po: On public datasets with three different model architectures, FedBridge accelerates convergence 6.3x and improves accuracy 6.2%-17.7%, while cutting communication overhead 89.51%-96.13% and memory overhead 48.12%-61.77%. It enables federated learning across heterogeneous clients, making federation practical for real-world deployments.
